faq: What access do you need to my code?
A repository invite, such as GitHub or Bitbucket, and the steps to build the app. We work on a branch and never push to your main branch. We never ask for passwords.
What if the codebase is old or messy?
We read it before we start. If a safe change needs bigger repairs, we tell you what and why, and keep the work to what you ordered. Large refactors are quoted separately.
Can you fix a crash I cannot reproduce?
We try. With crash logs from Xcode, TestFlight or a crash tool, we can often trace the cause. Without logs, a fix may only reduce the risk, and we say so clearly.
Do you work with UIKit as well as SwiftUI?
Yes. We follow what your app already uses and mix the two where it makes sense. We do not convert your whole app unless you order that as a separate job.
desc:
iOS feature development for existing apps means adding or fixing something in an app that is already live or in progress. Ecom Swift LLC reads your code, builds the change on a separate branch, tests it on real devices and hands it back as a pull request.

## What does iOS feature work include?

iOS feature work is a focused change to an existing iPhone app: a new screen, a flow such as checkout or onboarding, a connection to an existing API, or a bug fix. The work follows your project's structure, naming and style, so the result looks like your team wrote it.

It is different from a rebuild. We do not rewrite what already works. We touch only the parts the feature needs and leave the rest alone.

## Why careful feature work matters

Every change to a live app carries risk. A new screen can break navigation, a small fix can change behavior somewhere else, and code that ignores the project's conventions is hard for the next developer to read.

Apps also reach users through updates that cannot be pulled back instantly. A mistake in a release stays on phones until the next version is approved and installed. Careful work on a separate branch, with tests, keeps that risk small and visible before anything is merged.

## How new features and fixes affect your results

For customers, features are the reason to keep the app. A saved-items screen, a faster sign-in or a missing filter can change how often people return. For the business, a fixed bug can remove a steady source of support requests and one-star reviews.

The value comes from solving a specific problem well. A clear brief, a small scope and a tested result usually do more than a large feature that arrives late.

## What good feature delivery looks like

- A short written brief that states the goal, the screens involved and what done means.
- A review of the existing code before any change is made.
- Work on its own branch, never directly on your main branch.
- Code that follows your architecture, naming and file layout.
- Tests on a real iPhone and in simulators, across several iOS versions.
- Unit tests for any new logic, where your project has a test target.
- Handling of loading, empty and error states, not just the happy path.
- Analytics events for the new feature, when you ask for them.
- A pull request with plain notes on what changed and how to check it.

## How we work

You send a repository invitation and a short brief. We read the relevant code, confirm our understanding of the task in writing and note anything unclear. Then we build the change, test it and open a pull request for your team to review and merge.

The Basic package covers one small change or fix. Standard covers a new screen or flow with a connection to your API, tests on three iOS versions and unit tests. Premium covers a larger feature matched to your design, with analytics, UI tests and help with the release build.

We work with SwiftUI and UIKit, so we can follow whichever your project uses.

## Bugs you cannot reproduce

Some crashes only appear on certain devices or for certain accounts. We start with crash logs, user reports and the steps leading to the failure, then try to reproduce the problem on matching iOS versions. If we cannot reproduce it, we say so and describe what we tried, rather than guessing at a cause.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Describe the feature in terms of what the user should be able to do.
- Share designs, API documentation and test accounts up front.
- Tell us about parts of the code that are fragile or unfinished.
- Review the pull request promptly, while the work is fresh.
- Keep your branch protection rules in place.

**Avoid:**
- Changing the brief halfway through the work.
- Asking for several unrelated features in a single request.
- Sending a repository with secrets and keys stored in plain text.
- Merging without running your own build.
- Assuming a small visual change has no effect on other screens.

## Who this is for

A company with a small in-house team that is stretched on other work can hand over a well-defined feature. A founder with an older app and no developer can have bugs fixed one at a time. An agency may need extra capacity for a client app during a busy release.

## What we need from you

We need access to the repository as a collaborator, a written brief and any design files or API notes. A test account and a working build setup help us a great deal. We never need your passwords, and we do not need access to your App Store Connect account unless the work includes release support, in which case a limited role is enough.
